extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of English/literary criticism; critics and readers learning practical interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for training readers and critics to interpret literary (and discursive) texts accurately by analysing kinds of meaning, diagnosing misinterpretation, and teaching techniques to improve understanding. Emphasises classroom/group exercises, theory of meaning, and habits of mental suppleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling — undergo vs think of
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two important senses in which we can 'understand' the feeling of a passage: we can either undergo the same feeling ourselves or we can think of the feeling (i.e. consider it cognitively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms of understanding are fallible; in witnessing drama we may think of characters' feelings while undergoing the action's feeling. Simple arousal (e.g. cadence of a phrase) can produce feeling directly without intermediary thought. Be alert to mistakes in both emulative (adoptive) and reflective (perceptual) modes of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone — adopt vs perceive
rubrics_metrics.description: Our apprehension of tone (the speaker's attitude) may be either by adopting the attitude (thus 'recognising' it experientially) or by perceiving/reflecting upon it (recognising it in another sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone often invites a complimentary attitude from the reader; confusion between adopting and perceiving tone can mislead interpretation. Distinguish when your response is sympathy/adoption and when it is critical perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention — recognition vs thinking-of
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'recognise' an intention is not the same as to think of it; the actual arousal of recognising intention can be direct or mediated by awareness of sense or intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple intentions (especially self-regarding) may be recognised directly, but complex intentions require careful study of sense to avoid grotesque mistakes. Do not conflate immediate sense of intention with analysed inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and proportion among contributory meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: A full understanding requires not only correct thought, feeling, tone and recognition of intention, but that these contributory meanings appear in their right order and proportion to one another and that their interdependence, sequence and interrelations are seized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether feeling, thought, tone and intention are balanced: e.g., if feeling overly governs thought or vice versa, or if feeling is presented to cajole the reader (tone) or to curry favour with intention, the passage may fail. Authors may conceal such imbalance or avow it — the tone of any avowal is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernment (holistic formation) vs intellectual analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Discernment is the formation in the receptive mind of a whole condition of feeling and awareness corresponding to the original meaning; this is not identical to an intellectual analysis of that Total Meaning into its contributories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis is nevertheless necessary for discernment: practice in analytic exercises should aim to produce the capacity to form the holistic condition. Teaching should target both the analytic skills and the ability to re-form the whole meaning in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice in analysis to improve discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic practice (analysis) might lead to improvement in the capacity to discern whole meanings, though conventional parsing/paraphrasing are inadequate forms of such practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design exercises beyond mere parsing — ones that illuminate forms of meaning, ambiguity and psychological process. Group protocols and duplication of errors help students detect and correct their own misreadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use group exposure/publicity to reveal misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinterpretations are best exposed and made instructive through group demonstration and systematic publicity, since seeing others' errors makes us quicker to detect and challenge our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat wild interpretations of others not as mere incompetence but as real dangers you might also fall into. Press misreadings home in group settings so they shake complacency and provide diagnostic evidence of common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gain diagnostic capacity to detect interpretive errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should acquire powers of diagnosis: an understanding of the risks that interpretations run and an ability to detect what has actually occurred in a reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to recognise typical error-patterns, trace causes of misunderstanding, and practise methods for determining whether a reading stems from ambiguity, temperament, or misuse of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach theory of interpretation as a distinct subject
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry into language and interpretation — distinct from grammar, logician's or philologist's studies — should be recognised as a vital branch of research and taught systematically in schools and universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop instruments, nomenclature and simplified theory suitable for instruction; start with advanced classes and experiment with curricula. The lack of existing professional instruments is a gap to be filled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study how language works — the psychology of speech-situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning a language is not enough: one must study how it works — the kinds of meaning language handles, their connections and interferences, i.e., the psychology of the speech-situation rather than merely syntax or lexicography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus teaching on kinds of meaning, processes of abstraction, and how terms change across contexts. This study will aid understanding across prose, poetry and other disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reading value by direct training
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct training in interpretation can greatly increase the value of time spent in extensive reading, and a slight improvement in understanding justifies allocating some reading time to instruction in interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge the current reliance on fragmented incidental training; design short, practical exercises that deliver durable improvements in reading comprehension across subjects (economics, psychology, law, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental suppleness rather than rigid frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: The desirable critical mind is supple: it can shift viewpoint and carry over results across differing definitions and frameworks while keeping orientation; rigidity (the 'militarist' solution) fails because others cannot be forced to adopt our framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train students to hold multiple frameworks and to perform systematic transformations between them without confusion. Avoid teaching that forces all material into one doctrinal frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage ambiguity of abstract terms by multiple-definition technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract terms are inevitably ambiguous; sound criticism requires recognising multiple related meanings and being prepared to compare a given opinion as it is applied to many matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the habit of stating definitions explicitly ('I am defining X as...') and of carrying several mutually incompatible definitions in mind simultaneously. Use comparative applications to expose equivocations; avoid assuming one's own definition is the only legitimate one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mystification; explain what can be explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish genuine mystery from spurious mysteriousness arising from confusion; explanations that are possible should be given, because gross misunderstandings are a major enemy of poetry and prose alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not romanticise muddled-mindedness as 'poetic.' Where explanation is possible, employ it to clarify poetry and prose; reserve the label 'mystery' for genuinely inexplicable aspects (e.g., the will's choices), but do not use mystery as an excuse for ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise subjectivity without abandoning value judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to literature are subjective psychological events determined by needs and resources of minds, but this subjectivity does not eliminate the possibility of better or worse responses; criticism concerns relative values of states of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit differences of temperament and evolving personal outlooks; acknowledge that disagreement may persist. Aim to clarify whether disputes stem from misunderstanding or from differing evaluative orientations, and judge accordingly.
